Landing Pages and Ad Review: Why Yours Gets Rejected

Growth

In short: A landing page does one job for one source and is reviewed by the ad platform before the visitor sees it. To pass and convert, match the ad, disclose the business, make compliant claims, answer the visitor's doubts, and never show reviewers and users different pages.

Key points

  • Pages fail review most often for missing business information, unsupported claims, and category signals reviewers treat as restricted.
  • Words like yield, returns, weight or winnings sort a page into a restricted category before a human reads it.
  • Disguising the category or swapping content after review is the fastest route to a permanent ban and regulator attention.
  • A passing page repeats the clicked promise, shows the action above the fold, answers key doubts with proof, and lists business identity.
  • Apply the same compliance library to affiliate, creator and email landing pages, and capture an email address.

A landing page is the page a visitor arrives at from a particular source: an ad, a creator's link, an affiliate placement, an email. It exists to do one thing, and it is reviewed by two audiences before it does it: the platform's reviewer, and the person who arrives.

For companies in reviewed categories, the first audience is where most landing pages fail.

What a landing page is for

One source, one message, one action. A visitor who clicked an ad about a savings account should land on a page about that account, not on the homepage. The page should confirm they are in the right place, state the offer, answer the two or three doubts that stop people, provide proof, and ask for a single action. Everything else is a distraction, and on a page with a specific job, distraction is measured in lost conversions.

How ad platforms review it

Every major platform reviews the landing page as well as the ad, and rejects the pair if the page violates policy. Reviewers and classifiers look for: a match between what the ad promised and what the page shows; a working, complete, professional page rather than a shell; clear disclosure of who is behind it, with a real business name, address, and contact; prohibited or restricted claims, especially about money, health, and outcomes; required disclaimers, licenses, or registration details for the category; a privacy policy and terms; no misleading urgency, fake countdowns, or manufactured scarcity; and no attempt to show reviewers one page and users another.

Pages fail review most often for missing business information, unsupported claims, and category signals the reviewer treats as restricted regardless of the copy.

Why restricted-category pages get rejected

The categories the platforms review, financial products, crypto, health, supplements, gambling, dating, are reviewed against stricter claim rules, and the page is often what triggers the classification. A page that mentions yield, returns, weight, or winnings is sorted into the category by its vocabulary before a human reads it.

That is worth knowing, but it is not an invitation to disguise the page. Pages that hide the category, swap content after review, or route reviewers differently from users are the fastest way to a permanent account ban and, in regulated categories, to a regulator's attention. A page in a restricted category should be visibly and compliantly in that category, with the licenses, disclaimers, and disclosures the platform requires, and the company should know from the band map whether that platform will run it at all.

What a page that passes and converts contains

A headline that repeats the promise the visitor clicked on, in their words. One or two sentences on what changes for them. The action, visible without scrolling, with a label that says what happens next. The two or three most common doubts answered briefly: is my money safe, what does it cost, how long does it take. Proof matched to those doubts: the custodian, the license, the review, the number. Business identity in the footer: legal name, address, contact, registration. Required disclaimers and a privacy policy, linked. Speed, on mobile, because most reviewed-category traffic is mobile. Nothing else.

For channels other than ads

Affiliate, creator, and email traffic lands too, and those pages are not reviewed by a platform, which tempts companies to relax. Do not. The compliance library that governs the ads should govern every page, because regulators read landing pages and creators send their audiences there. And every page should ask for an email address before or after the main action, because the visitor arrived through a rented channel and the company should leave with something it owns.

lowob takeaway: A landing page does one job for one source and is reviewed by the platform before the visitor sees it. Match the ad, disclose the business, make compliant claims, answer the doubts, and never build a page designed to be read differently by reviewers and users.

Common questions

Why does my landing page keep getting rejected by ad platforms?

Most often for missing business information, unsupported claims, or category signals the reviewer treats as restricted regardless of the copy. Reviewers also check that the page matches the ad, is complete, has required disclaimers, a privacy policy and terms, and avoids fake urgency.

Can I hide that my landing page is about crypto or finance to pass ad review?

No. Pages that hide the category, swap content after review, or route reviewers differently from users are the fastest way to a permanent account ban and, in regulated categories, to a regulator's attention.

What should a high-converting landing page contain?

A headline repeating the promise the visitor clicked on, a line on what changes for them, a visible action, brief answers to the two or three most common doubts with matching proof, business identity in the footer, required disclaimers, and fast mobile load.
